input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

output:
We presented a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes explicit evidence use and machine-readable section outputs. The central elements of the workflow are (i) an explicit document/section graph and a leaf-first writing schedule that decomposes writing dependencies, (ii) an evidence-retrieval and injection protocol that attaches provenance to assertions at section time, (iii) a strict JSON schema and automated validation checks for each generated section, and (iv) an assembly procedure that maps validated section outputs into a LaTeX manuscript with a refs.bib file. These components are intended to make generated text more auditable, to reduce the surface area for unsupported assertions, and to simplify post-hoc editing through structured, reparable outputs.

Our experimental evaluation was intentionally conservative in scope and interpretation. Rather than claim broad generalization, we treat the reported experiments as a focused probe of whether graph-aware sectioning and evidence-aware prompts can improve citation fidelity and reduce unsupported assertions relative to a linear prompting baseline within the tested domains. The empirical findings reported in this work should therefore be read as preliminary: they motivate further, larger-scale evaluation rather than definitive performance guarantees across domains and retrieval configurations.

We also emphasize design principles and practical artifacts that are broadly useful regardless of experimental scale:
- A document-graph scheduler that makes explicit which sections should be written first to maximize evidence availability and minimize downstream inconsistency.
- An evidence-injection protocol that preserves provenance metadata and encourages the generator to anchor claims to specific sources.
- A JSON-constrained output format that enables schema validation, automated repair heuristics, and straightforward integration with LaTeX/bib workflows for reproducible manuscript assembly.

Limitations and caveats are central to our conclusions. The current study is constrained by dataset scale, domain coverage, and dependence on retrieval quality; these constraints limit claims about generalization. Additionally, automated validation can detect many, but not all, classes of unsupported reasoning or subtle misattributions; human review and targeted audits remain necessary components of any production pipeline. Finally, we did not attempt to demonstrate novelty relative to a comprehensive set of prior works in document planning and citation-aware generation; confirming the method’s novelty and broader comparative performance requires more extensive literature-grounded benchmarking.

For future work we recommend three directions that follow directly from our findings and design goals:
- Larger-scale, multi-domain evaluations using community-shared datasets and standardized audit protocols to quantify gains in citation fidelity and factual consistency.
- Improvements to retrieval and ranking (including hybrid human–AI retrieval loops) to increase evidence coverage for low-resource or emerging topics.
- Tooling for mixed-initiative review, where structured section outputs and provenance metadata are exposed to human authors and reviewers to enable efficient correction, acceptance, or extension of generated content.

In closing, this work argues for workflows that combine document-structure priors with strict, evidence-centered prompting and machine-readable outputs. We advocate conservative reporting practices—explicit source citations for factual assertions and cautious interpretation of experimental gains—and provide artefacts intended to make long-form generation more auditable and easier to iteratively improve. Continued work along the directions above is required to move from preliminary, domain-limited results to broadly reliable tools for scientific writing.
